facts.text: ISO 3450:2011 covers wheeled earth-moving machines and rubber-tracked machines with maximum speeds of at least 20 km/h.
facts.quote: ISO 3450:2011 covers wheeled earth-moving machines and rubber-tracked machines with maximum speeds of at least 20 km/h.

facts.text: ISO 3450:2011 defines stopping distance from the start of brake-control actuation to standstill, excluding operator reaction time but including brake-system response time.
facts.quote: It defines stopping distance from the start of brake-control actuation to standstill, so the figure excludes operator reaction time but includes brake-system response time.

facts.text: Under ISO 3450:2011, machines limited by design to under 6 km/h meet the safe-state requirement if any braking system stops them within the stated distances.
facts.quote: Machines limited by design to under 6 km/h meet the safe-state requirement if any braking system stops them within the stated distances.

facts.text: The 2011 edition of ISO 3450 was reviewed and confirmed in 2022.
facts.quote: The 2011 edition was reviewed and confirmed in 2022.

facts.text: Crawler machines at 20 km/h or less fall under ISO 10265:2008.
facts.quote: Crawler machines at 20 km/h or less fall under ISO 10265:2008, confirmed in 2025.

facts.text: ISO 10265:2008 was confirmed in 2025.
facts.quote: ISO 10265:2008, confirmed in 2025.

facts.text: The New South Wales Resources Regulator's undated brake-formula guidance is built on ISO 3450:1996 and AS 2958.1.
facts.quote: The New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance (undated; built on ISO 3450:1996 and AS 2958.1)

facts.text: The New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance proposes minimum mean safe net decelerations in service of 0.60 m/s² for service brakes and 0.30 m/s² for secondary brakes.
facts.quote: proposes a minimum mean safe net deceleration of 0.60 m/s² for service brakes in service and 0.30 m/s² for secondary brakes

facts.text: For type testing, the New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance proposes minimum mean safe net decelerations of 0.75 m/s² for service brakes and 0.40 m/s² for secondary brakes.
facts.quote: raised to 0.75 m/s² and 0.40 m/s² for type testing.

facts.text: A worked example in the New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance requires a 100 t rigid dump truck at 40 km/h, with a 20% design grade and tested on a 9% grade, to reach at least 1.79 m/s² and stop within 34.4 m.
facts.quote: A 100 t rigid dump truck (40 km/h, 20% design grade) tested on a 9% grade must reach at least 1.79 m/s² and stop within 34.4 m.

facts.text: A worked example in the New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance specifies 3.13 m/s² and a stopping distance of 30.82 m for a 25 t articulated dump truck at 50 km/h on level ground.
facts.quote: A 25 t articulated dump truck at 50 km/h on level ground needs 3.13 m/s² and 30.82 m.

facts.text: A worked example in the New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance specifies 2.24 m/s² and a stopping distance of 42.25 m at 32 km/h for a 60 t articulated dump truck tested at 50 t for a 13% site grade.
facts.quote: A 60 t articulated dump truck tested at 50 t for a 13% site grade needs 2.24 m/s² and 42.25 m at 32 km/h.

facts.text: The New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake formulas assume traction and no skidding.
facts.quote: All of these formulas assume traction and no skidding

facts.text: The New South Wales Resources Regulator's brake-formula guidance is a proposal rather than an adopted rule.
facts.quote: the document is a proposal rather than an adopted rule.

facts.text: United States in-service brake tests for surface metal and nonmetal mines under 30 CFR 56.14101, Table M-1, compute maximum stopping distances using a constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s² (about 2.94 m/s²), weight-dependent system response time, and one second of operator response time.
facts.quote: compute maximum stopping distances from a constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s² (about 2.94 m/s²), plus a system response time that grows with weight class

facts.text: Table M-1 of United States regulation 30 CFR 56.14101 uses brake-system response times of 0.5 s up to 36,000 lb, 1.0 s to 70,000 lb, 1.5 s to 140,000 lb, 2.0 s to 250,000 lb, 2.25 s to 400,000 lb, and 2.5 s above 400,000 lb (about 181 t).
Under United States regulation 30 CFR 56.14101, equipment up to 36,000 lb must stop within 34 ft (10.4 m) from 10 mph (16 km/h) and within 89 ft (27.1 m) from 20 mph (32 km/h).
facts.quote: equipment up to 36,000 lb must stop within 34 ft (10.4 m) from 10 mph (16 km/h) and within 89 ft (27.1 m) from 20 mph (32 km/h).

facts.text: United States regulation 30 CFR 56.14101 requires brakes capable of stopping and holding equipment with its typical load on the maximum grade it travels.
facts.quote: The rule also requires brakes capable of stopping and holding the equipment with its typical load on the maximum grade it travels.

facts.text: UN Regulation No. 152, paragraphs 5.2.1.2 and 5.2.2.2, requires car automatic emergency braking to demand at least 5.0 m/s² from the vehicle's service braking system; this is a braking demand, not measured deceleration, and is on-road evidence.
facts.quote: requires "a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s² to the service braking system of the vehicle" (paragraphs 5.2.1.2 and 5.2.2.2). That is a demand, not a measured deceleration, and it is on-road.

facts.text: A haul-road bunching patent from Caterpillar's field expresses maximum deceleration as a = P/(v·m) − g·sin θ, making the power-limited retarder nature of large-truck braking explicit: available deceleration falls with speed and mass and is further reduced by downgrade.
facts.quote: writes maximum deceleration as a = P/(v·m) − g·sin θ, making the power-limited (retarder) nature of large-truck braking explicit: available deceleration falls with speed and mass and is reduced further by downgrade.
